synopsis: ISO 12100 is the foundational Type-A machinery-safety standard, defining safety terminology and the general method for assessing and reducing risk [f12374, f11962, f12375, f15261]. Its method starts by defining machine and use limits, identifying hazards, and estimating and evaluating risk, then requires reduction in strict order: inherently safe design, safeguarding and complementary protective measures, and information for use [f12378, f12379, f15261]. Automatic braking belongs to the second step rather than replacing safe design or site controls; consequently, identical braking algorithms can yield different safety results under different traffic rules and pedestrian controls [f12380, f12381, f12387]. Chapter 3 and the glossary consistently place ISO 21815-3:2023 beneath this framework as a machine-specific Type-C standard; the glossary says Type-C standards take precedence and distinguishes them from generic control-system standards such as ISO 13849 [f2165, f2664, f12377, f15007]. The mining nine-layer model reflects the same sequencing: understand site design and operating controls at Levels 1–7 before adding advisory technology at Level 8 and intervention technology at Level 9, while residual risk remains the risk left after protective measures [f12386, f12140].
